en: Because of the assault of the threefold suffering, there arises a desire to know the means for its removal. If it is argued that such inquiry is purposeless since a remedy is already seen in the world, we say no, because that remedy is neither absolute nor final. (SK 2)

The scriptural (ānuśravika) [means] is like the perceptible (dṛṣṭavat), for it is characterized by impurity, destruction, and excess; superior to that is the means which is the opposite of that, arising from the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the Knower.
Root-nature is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and modification;
the group of sixteen is modification only; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3)

Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony—these three types of means of valid cognition are accepted because all means of valid cognition are established by them; for the establishment of the objects of cognition occurs through the means of valid cognition. (SK 5) Authoritative testimony is the word of a reliable person. (Editor’s emendation)

Perception is the determinative cognition of each respective object; inference is said to be of three kinds, preceded by the mark (liṅga) and that which possesses the mark (liṅgin); and authoritative verbal testimony is the word of a reliable person.
However, the cognition of supersensible objects arises from inference based on what is perceived in a general way;
and that which is unestablished even by that [inference] is established through the scripture of a reliable person (*āptāgama*).
[The object] is not perceived due to excessive distance, proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind,
subtlety, obstruction, being overwhelmed, and blending with similar things. (SK 7–8)
Its non-perception is due to its subtlety, not due to its non-existence; it is perceived through its effects.
And that effect, beginning with the Great One (mahat), is both dissimilar and similar to its source, primordial nature (prakṛti). 1. *upalabdheḥ* J, V 2. *tac ca* 3. *sa-rūpaṃ*
And that [Prakṛti], consisting of the Great One (Mahat) and so forth, is both similar and dissimilar [to Puruṣa]. (SK 9)

The effect exists [prior to its production] because (1) that which is non-existent cannot be produced, (2) there is the grasping of a material cause, (3) everything is not possible from everything, (4) the capable [cause] produces only that for which it is capable, and (5) because of the nature of the cause.
[Furthermore, the effect] is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, and indicative.
The Manifest is composed of parts, dependent, and subordinate; the Unmanifest is the opposite.

The Manifest consists of the three qualities, is non-discriminative, is an object, is common, is insentient, and has the nature of productivity; the Pradhāna is likewise. The Spirit (Puruṣa) is the reverse of these and is also like that [in certain respects].

The guṇas consist of pleasure, pain, and dejection; they serve the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint; and their functions are characterized by mutual suppression, support, production, and union.
Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. And their functioning is for the sake of a purpose, like a lamp.
For non-discrimination and the rest are established by reason of the presence of the three *guṇas* and the absence of their opposite;
and because the effect consists of the qualities of its cause, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is also established.

S; -ādir hi siddhaṃ K 2 viparyaye V Because of the finite magnitude of diverse things, because of their commonality, because of their activity through power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-differentiation of the multiform universe, [the Primal Cause] is established.

There exists a cause for the manifest, which is the unmanifest; it proceeds from the three qualities (guṇas), from their conjunction, and from transformation, like water, due to the particularity of the substratum of each respective quality.
Because it is for the sake of another through aggregation, because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth, and because of presiding over [the elements].
The Puruṣa exists because there must be an experiencer and because of the activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya).
[He exists] also because of the specific determination of births, deaths, and instruments, and because of their non-simultaneous activity.
The plurality of Puruṣas is established precisely from the absence of the three guṇas [in them]. Birth [arises] from the three guṇas and so forth.
And from this absence of error, the following qualities of this Puruṣa are established: its state of being a witness,
its isolation (kaivalya), its neutrality, its status as a seer, and its lack of agency.

Because of the absence of the state of being a questioner [in the Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body), through conjunction with that [Puruṣa], appears as if it were sentient; and likewise,
while the *guṇas* are the actual agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent himself.

The qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception, and likewise the Pradhāna exists for the sake of liberation (kaivalya). Like a lame man and a blind man, there is a union of both; from that [union] proceeds creation. 1. *kaivalyārtham* V2 2. *api* J, M, V 3. *bhavatīti* G (note) 4. *udāsīnā* V2 5. *tatkṛtaḥ* G (note) 6. *sargaḥ* G (note)
The Great Principle (mahat) arises from primordial nature (prakṛti) for the sake of perception and for the sake of isolation;
Therefore, there is a group of sixteen;
and from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements arise.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is determination; its sattvic form consists of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, while its tamasic form is the opposite of this.
From that [intellect] proceeds the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which is self-conceit; from it, the twofold creation proceeds.
The group of eleven consists of those [five] alone plus the five [sensory objects], and the group of five consists of the sense organs alone.
(1) The elevenfold group is that of the senses;
(2) *mātra* is found in J, M, V, and K.

From the *vaikṛta* ego arises the group of eleven characterized by *sattva*; from the *bhūtādi* ego arises the group of five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) characterized by *tamas*; and from the *taijasa* ego arise both.
and V say that the sense organs of cognition— known as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin— and the organs of action— speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals— are called the [eleven] faculties.
1. *śrotra-* V1, M; *karṇa-* Y, M (var); 2–3. [The organs] called skin, eye, tongue, and nose V1, Y, M; 3. *sparśanāni* V2.
The sense organs consist of both [types of elements]; here, the mind is characterized by volition and is an organ due to its commonality with them.
Their diversity arises from specific transformations of the *guṇas* and from the distinction between the external [objects] and the [internal] senses.
In this context, the mind is that which forms intentions;
it is declared to be a sense-organ in two ways.
Because its objects pertain to the three times internally, it therefore functions in both ways.

2. Regarding the objects of apprehension (grāhya): it is held that the function (vṛtti) of the five [sense organs] is mere observation (ālocana-mātra) of [their respective objects], such as sound and so forth; and those of the other five are speech, grasping, locomotion, excretion, and pleasure.
the three [mental factors] function according to their own specific characteristics; this is their uncommon mode of operation.
The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa.
Their simultaneous activity of the four [organs] and their sequential activity have been specified.
Whether [the object] is seen or unseen, the activity of the triad is preceded by that [perception];
for they each undertake their own respective activity, which is caused by the mutual intention [of the others].
The purpose of the person alone is the cause; no instrument is set in motion by anything else.
The thirteenfold instrument performs the functions of bringing about, sustaining, and manifesting.
it is to be taken away, to be maintained, and to be manifested.

The internal organ is threefold; the external is tenfold, being designated as the objects of the [three internal organs]. The external organ functions in the present time, while the internal organ functions in all three times. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 34)
Among those, the five organs of cognition have as their objects both the specific and the non-specific;
speech has sound as its object, while the remaining [four] have all five [elements] as their objects.

Since that intellect (*buddhi*), together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), perceives every object, therefore the threefold instrument is the gatekeeper, while the remaining ones are the gates.
These specific qualities of the *guṇas* are like lamps, distinct from one another.
Having illuminated the entire purpose of the Puruṣa, they deliver it to the intellect (buddhi).
Since the intellect accomplishes every experience for the Puruṣa,
it alone further distinguishes the subtle difference between Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
1. From that [Mahat] arise the subtle elements (tanmātras), which are the non-specific (aviśeṣa); from those five [subtle elements] arise the five gross elements.
These are known as the specific (viśeṣa), being calm, terrible, and delusive.
these subtle distinctions born of mother and father, together with those that are abundant, are of three kinds.
Of these, the subtle elements are constant; those born of mother and father cease.

The *liṅga* (the transmigrating body), beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the subtle elements, is produced first, is unattached, constant, devoid of experience, and migrates, being perfumed by dispositions (*bhāva*).

Just as a formless enjoyment [cannot exist] without a substratum, and just as a shadow cannot exist without a post or the like, so too the subtle body (*liṅga*) does not remain without a support, being devoid of the specific elements (*viśeṣas*).
Just as [a cloth] does not exist without threads,
this [world] exists for the sake of the purpose of the Puruṣa through the connection of causes and their effects.
Due to its connection with the sovereignty of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the subtle body (*liṅga*) manifests like an actor;
so too do the innate dispositions (*bhāvas*) and the qualities (*dharmas*) such as virtue (*dharma*), which are both natural and modified.
The embryo and other such stages are observed to reside in both the instruments (the senses) and the body (the effect).
By means of merit (dharma), there is upward movement; by means of demerit (adharma), downward movement occurs.
Through knowledge, liberation is attained; conversely, bondage is held to result from its opposite.
From dispassion comes dissolution into primordial nature; from passionate attachment, transmigration occurs.
From passion comes sovereignty without obstruction; from its opposite, the reverse of that. (V1, M read: "from passionate attachment, transmigration occurs.")
This is the evolution of the objective world (pratyaya-sarga), known as error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment;
it arises from the mutual suppression of the imbalance of the guṇas, and its subdivisions are fifty.
K; by means of the crushing, V2, V1 (comm.), J, M; in the crushing, V1 3 [missing], V2, V1, J, M.

There are five varieties of error; and due to the deficiency of the organs, there are twenty-eight varieties of incapacity; contentment is ninefold, and attainment is eightfold. 1. *aśaktiḥ* V1, G (except for D), J. 2. *bhedās* V1, G (except for D), J.
The division of *tamas* is eightfold; that of *moha* is likewise eightfold; *mahāmoha* is tenfold;
*tāmisra* is eighteenfold; and so too is *andhatāmisra*.
The eleven obstructions of the faculties (indriya-vadha), together with the obstructions of the intellect (buddhi-vadha), are designated as incapacity (aśakti).
There are seventeen such obstructions of the intellect, which arise from the inversion of contentment (tuṣṭi) and accomplishment (siddhi).
1. Destruction (vadhā) G; 2. Taught (upadiṣṭā) J, K; 3. Seventeenfold (saptadaśa-dhā) G; and (ca) J, K; but (tu) D; 4.
Intellect (buddhiḥ) Y; 5. Errors (viparyayāḥ) J; errors (viparyayāḥ) K.

The nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*) are considered to be four internal—namely those called nature (*prakṛti*), acquisition (*upādāna*), time (*kāla*), and fortune (*bhāgya*)—and five external, resulting from the cessation of objects.
Y, M; *adhyātmikāś* K 2; *bhāga* V1, G(F), D 3; *-ramāt pañca ca* Y, V, K; *-ramāt pañca* J.
—ramāś ca pañca V1, G(D); —ramāḥ pañca D; nava ca M 5; —hitāḥ G(D, F).

Reasoning, oral instruction, study, and the three forms of the destruction of suffering; the acquisition of friends, and generosity—these are the eight accomplishments (siddhis). The first [set] among these accomplishments is the threefold restraint (aṅkuśa), which consists of the three types of obstacles to suffering. 1. *Vighāta-trayaṃ* (the three obstacles) as in V1. 2. *Siddhayo 'ṣṭau* (the eight accomplishments). 3. *Siddheḥ* (of the accomplishment). 4. *Pūrvo 'ṅkuśas tri-vidhaḥ* (the preceding restraint is threefold). 5. *Vighāta-trayaṃ* (the three obstacles) as in V1.
M 2: Siddhayoga; K 3: Siddhi V2; V1: *siddhe*.
Without the dispositions (*bhāva*) there is no mark (*liṅga*), and without the mark there is no manifestation of the dispositions (*bhāvanirvṛtti*).
[The creation proceeds as twofold: that which is called the mark and that which is called the disposition. (Therefore, the creation proceeds in two ways.)
Through the state of being, there is the cessation of the marks;
divine, which is of eight kinds, and animal, which is of five kinds.
And the human realm is of one kind; in brief, this is the elemental creation.
-as, -aś, -aś] 1 gods V1 2 animals V1; belonging to the animal realm J 3 [missing] G(D)
4. Human, V; 5. But one, G(D); 6. This, threefold, G(D).
The creation at the top is characterized by an abundance of *sattva*, and that at the root is characterized by an abundance of *tamas*;
in the middle, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, it is characterized by an abundance of *rajas*.

In this regard, the conscious person (cetanaḥ puruṣaḥ) undergoes the suffering caused by old age and death because the subtle body (liṅga) does not cease; therefore, suffering is its very nature (svabhāva). (Note: Regarding the variant readings, the commentary on verse 1 indicates that the reading "atra janma" [here, birth] was found in the versions of V1, Y, and M.)

2 [missing] V2 3 Even so, V1 4 in brief, V1, Y, M this undertaking— beginning with the Great One (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa) and the gross elements (bhūta), produced by primordial nature (prakṛti)— is for the sake of the liberation of each individual soul; though it appears to be for its own sake, it is in fact for the sake of another.
The modified creation of beings proceeds for its own sake,
just as the flow of milk from the ignorant [cow] occurs for the purpose of the growth of the calf.

The primary cause (pradhāna) proceeds in such a manner for the sake of the liberation of the person (puruṣa). Just as people engage in activities for the purpose of satisfying their longing, so too does the unmanifest proceed for the sake of the liberation of the person.

Just as a dancer ceases her dance after displaying the various colors for the sake of the spectator's liberation, so too does primordial nature (*prakṛti*) cease once it has manifested itself to the person (*puruṣa*).
She turns away from the man who does not reciprocate her kindness despite her various efforts;
though she is virtuous, she acts for the sake of that one who is devoid of virtue, pursuing what is useless for him.
Through various kinds of services, Prakṛti acts [for the Puruṣa];
yet it is my conviction that there is nothing more delicate than she.
Once she has been seen by the Puruṣa with the thought, "I have been seen," she does not come into his sight again.
Therefore, truly, no one is bound; nor is anyone released, nor does anyone transmigrate.
It is *prakṛti*, depending on various substrates, that transmigrates, is bound, and is released.
(G, C, D read "is released" for "no one is released").

By means of these seven forms alone, Nature binds herself by herself.
And she alone liberates [the person] with respect to the goal of the person (puruṣārtha) in a single manner.
Thus, V1, M; thus, V2, G.
2 With respect to the goal of the person, M.
through the repeated practice of reality, the person realizes: "I am not, nothing is mine, and there is no I," without exception.
From the absence of error, pure and absolute knowledge arises.

By means of that, the Puruṣa— standing firm like a spectator— beholds Prakṛti, whose productivity has ceased and which, by the force of the object [of experience], has desisted from its sevenfold form.
"I have seen her"—thus one [the Puruṣa] becomes indifferent; "I have been seen"—thus the other [Prakṛti] ceases.
Even when there is a union between these two, there is no further purpose for creation. [Note:
The variants indicate that the Puruṣa is "standing on the stage" (raṅga-stha) and "is indifferent" (upekṣate).]
Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, when dharma and the other factors no longer function as causes,
he remains with his body sustained by the force of past impressions (*saṃskāra*), like the whirling of a potter's wheel.
When the dissolution of the body has occurred and the primary cause (pradhāna) has ceased its activity because its purpose has been fulfilled,
one attains both the absolute and the final state of liberation (kaivalya).
This secret knowledge regarding the goal of the Puruṣa was fully proclaimed by the Supreme Seer.
and dissolution of all beings are investigated.
